title: Where year-end shoppers are buying this year, and how to reach them
summary: Discover how Q4 shoppers move across retailers, devices, and channels, and how marketers can adapt their strategies to reach them.
body_markdown:
When most brands approach channel allocation, the natural starting point is last year’s results. The channels that performed best typically get the most budget allocated again.


That instinct makes sense, and for many brands last year’s results are the most reliable signal available. But last year’s shopper data suggests the approach can leave gaps. The channels that performed last year may still be working, but year-end shoppers move across more retailers, devices, and touchpoints than any single channel can cover, and a plan built only on last year’s winners can miss where a meaningful share of purchases happen.


### **How do shoppers move during the peak season?**


Criteo’s


[Year-End Shopping Decoded report](https://www.criteo.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/26-Year-End-Shopping-Decoded-Global.pdf) analyzes shopping behavior through the year-end shopping season using commerce data from hundreds of partner brands and retailers. Three trends from the 2025 season stand out:


- **Between retailers:** When US shoppers browse a category across several retailers, they see six brands on average, compared with two when they stay inside one store. Europe and Japan show the same pattern on a smaller scale.


- **Between devices:** Mobile accounted for 61% of US sales during Cyber 6 (the six days from Thanksgiving through the following Tuesday), up from 58% the year before. Mobile share also rose in Japan (to 59%) and EMEA (to 39%).


- **Over time:** A quarter of shoppers start researching nearly two months before they buy (57 days in the US, 59 in Europe, and 76 in Japan), while the fastest quarter decides within minutes.


On their own, each of these looks like a familiar trend. Together, they describe a shopper who rarely stays in one place long enough for any one channel to reach them. That has a practical consequence: the question isn’t which channel won last year, but whether your plan can follow the same shopper across retailers, screens, and weeks.


### **Why are AI assistants becoming a peak-season channel?**


AI assistants are one of the fastest-growing new channels of the past two peak end of year shopping seasons. According to Adobe Analytics data, traffic to US retail sites from generative AI tools rose 693% year over year during the 2025 holidays,


¹


and shoppers arriving from those tools converted 31% better than visitors from other sources.


²


The base is still smaller than search or email, but shoppers are clearly using AI assistants to compare products, check prices, and find gift ideas. Many advertisers, particularly larger ones, have been slower to follow, often because best practices and measurement for the channel are still taking shape. That gives early movers an advantage this season, one that is likely to narrow by next year.


This is the first year-end season in which advertisers need to plan for AI assistants as a channel, and Criteo has been running ChatGPT Ads with advertisers throughout 2026. In our


[recent webinar with OpenAI](https://experiences.criteo.com/peak-season-webinar) , we shared what we’ve learned about the channel heading into the peak shopping season: it reaches shoppers your other channels don’t, holiday and festive season shopping on ChatGPT follows the same seasonal curve as traditional channels, and more creative variation means more delivery, which is what Criteo’s Prompt Smart is built to support.


### **How can advertisers cover more channels without fragmenting their plans?**


The aim is to be present where shoppers are going and to manage those channels as one plan, rather than to spend more on the channels that already perform. Four questions can help:


- **Is every channel covered?** Shoppers move between the open web, apps, social, CTV, and now AI assistants. For each, is there active spend, or an assumption that last year’s channels will capture the demand? Criteo can activate across all of them, including ChatGPT Ads.


- **Is one signal driving it?** The shopper comparing six brands across three retailers, in apps and on the web, is one person. Criteo connects those signals across channels to a single shopper, so real commerce signals, based on what people browse and buy across retailers, can inform every channel and the same in-market shopper is recognized wherever they appear. This is where Criteo Commerce Audiences can help you ensure you’re reaching shoppers who are actually on the journey to purchase, versus wasting spend on users who aren’t likely to convert.


- **Is the full journey visible?** Without cross-channel measurement, each channel reports its own version of the sale. Criteo now provides Path to Purchase reporting for open web, video and CTV, social, and OpenAI, so you can map the journey to conversion instead of only evaluating by last click, and identify which paths, channel mixes, and touchpoints produce the strongest outcomes.


- **For global brands, does the plan reflect regional timing?** US and European store trends moved in opposite directions last year, and Japan’s peak arrives earlier.


### **Putting it all together**


Last year’s winners are still a good starting point, but they only show where shoppers were, not where they’re going. This season, the practical move is to audit your coverage against how shoppers actually move (across retailers, screens, and weeks), add the channels you’re missing, with a small, controlled test where budget allows, and tie them together with one view of the in-market shopper so you’re not paying to reach the same person three times.


With Black Friday only weeks away, there’s still time to test, measure, and adjust before the peak.
